title: The admin console on the internet
brief: 18:25. A scan finds the container management dashboard answering on the public internet. It was set up in a hurry during a migration.
role: Platform engineer, reviewing a change on the Veltrix engineering team
insight: A management console reachable from anywhere, with the login it shipped with.
teaches: Management interfaces belong on a private network, behind single sign on and MFA
Remove default credentials and rotate anything already exposed
A secret path or a changed password on an open service is not access control

value.title: Container dashboard review

lines: allow tcp 8443 from 0.0.0.0/0     # migration, remove later

value.intro: You are on the internet. See what you can find, and what you can do with it.

attempts.label: Reach the dashboard from the office VPN
attempts.fixedResponse: HTTP 200  Sign in with your company account (SSO + MFA).

attempts.label: Find it from the internet
attempts.response:
ops-01.veltrix-logistics.com:8443  open
Container dashboard, version 2.7 detected.

It answers to the whole internet.
attempts.fixedResponse: ops-01.veltrix-logistics.com:8443  filtered. Not reachable from outside the company network.

attempts.label: Sign in with admin / admin
attempts.response:
HTTP 200
Signed in. You can start, stop and open a shell in any container, including the payments service.
attempts.fixedResponse: Not reachable from here. Sign in requires the company single sign on and a hardware key.

fix.prompt: Pick every change that takes it off the internet, puts proper sign in in front of it, and removes the default login.

options.label: Restrict it to the private network, or the VPN, and close the public port
code: + allow tcp 8443 from 10.20.0.0/16   # VPN and office
options.why: It cannot be found, or attacked, from the internet at all.

options.label: Put it behind single sign on with MFA
options.why: Access follows the person: their account, their second factor, and it is removed when they leave.

options.label: Delete the default account and rotate any credentials that were exposed
code: + # no local accounts; rotate keys the dashboard could read
options.why: It was open with a default login, so assume it was used, and change what it could reach.

options.label: Move it to a secret path so nobody finds it
options.why: Scanners and certificate logs reveal hosts and paths. A secret address is not a lock.

options.label: Change the admin password but leave it on the public internet
options.why: A better password on an open management console will be guessed, stuffed or phished, and every unpatched flaw in it is exposed too.

outcome.label: Read the vulnerable code first
outcome.what: Reading the code before attacking it tells you where to look, and why it fails.
outcome.ideal: reads the code under review before trying to break it.

outcome.label: Tried normal use first
outcome.what: Knowing what a good request looks like is how you spot a bad one.
outcome.ideal: establishes normal behaviour before testing the abnormal.

outcome.label: Checked normal use still works
outcome.what: A fix that breaks real users gets reverted, and the bug comes back.
outcome.ideal: tests that the fix did not break normal use.

exploit.objective: Reproduce the bug: read the Code tab, then use the Exploit tab on staging.
exploit.insight: A management console reachable from anywhere, with the login it shipped with.

label: Send this request: it breaks it
Open the Exploit tab

hint.text: Open the Workbench. Read the code, try normal use on the Exploit tab, then send the request that breaks it.

outcome.label: Reproduced the bug
outcome.what: The dashboard was open to the whole internet, and the shipped login still worked. From it you could open a shell in any container, including the payments service.
outcome.ideal: proves a bug is real before fixing it.

card.title: One search, one login, every container
body: The dashboard was open to the whole internet, and the shipped login still worked. From it you could open a shell in any container, including the payments service.
The firewall rule even says "migration, remove later".
card.ideal: reproduces a bug first, so the fix can be proved to work.

fix.objective: Fix it: pick the changes on the Fix tab that close the hole for good, then apply the patch.

label: Picked everything that fixes it? Apply the patch
Pick every change that fixes the cause
Open the Fix tab

hint.text: Pick every change that removes the cause. Avoid changes an attacker can walk around, and ones that do not touch the problem. Then Apply the patch.

outcome.label: Applied a real fix
outcome.what: Restricting it to the private network removes it from the internet entirely. Single sign on with a hardware key ties access to a person, and the default account is gone. Anything it could read gets rotated, because it was open for weeks.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause, not the symptom.

card.title: Not on the internet, not without you
body: Restricting it to the private network removes it from the internet entirely. Single sign on with a hardware key ties access to a person, and the default account is gone. Anything it could read gets rotated, because it was open for weeks.
Management interfaces are not for the public internet.
card.ideal: fixes the cause with the standard control, and adds defence in depth.

outcome.label: Applied a fix that can be bypassed
outcome.what: Hiding it on a secret path or choosing a stronger password still leaves a management console visible to attackers, with every flaw in it exposed. Scans find hosts by certificate and by port.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause instead of blocking one payload or hiding the symptom.

card.title: A better lock on the wrong door
body: Hiding it on a secret path or choosing a stronger password still leaves a management console visible to attackers, with every flaw in it exposed. Scans find hosts by certificate and by port.
Take it off the internet first.
card.ideal: fixes the cause, and knows why a blocklist or a hidden field is not a fix.

outcome.label: Applied a patch that was not enough
outcome.what: The patch missed part of the fix, or added a change that does not address the problem.

card.title: Not enough
body: The patch missed something that has to change, or included a change that does nothing for this bug. Open the Fix tab to see which options were right, missed, or wrong, and why.
A partial fix is the most dangerous kind: everyone assumes it is closed.

verify.objective: Prove it: re-run the exploit on the Exploit tab, then check normal use still works.

label: Send the exploit again: it should be blocked
Open the Exploit tab

hint.text: On the Exploit tab, send the exploit again. It should be blocked. Then send the normal request to check nothing broke.

outcome.label: Proved the exploit is blocked
outcome.what: The same request that worked before now fails, and normal use still works.
outcome.ideal: verifies a fix by re-running the exploit.

card.title: Fixed, and proved
body: You re-ran the exact request that broke it, and it is blocked. A fix you have not tested against the exploit is a hope, not a fix.
Add the exploit as an automated test so nobody can quietly bring the bug back.
card.ideal: turns the exploit into a regression test.

outcome.label: The exploit still works
outcome.what: The patch did not close the hole. The same kind of request still gets through.
outcome.ideal: never ships a fix without re-running the exploit.

card.title: Still open
body: The exploit still works after your patch. This is what happens when a fix blocks one payload, or hides a symptom, instead of removing the cause.
Go back over the Fix tab: it shows which options were right, and why the others fail.
card.ideal: verifies with the exploit before calling it fixed.
